promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Stellar classification and the H-R diagram

questions.q: Which sequence lists the main stellar spectral classes in order from hottest to coolest?
options: O, B, A, F, G, K, M
M, K, G, F, A, B, O
A, B, C, D, E, F, G
G, K, M, O, B, A, F
questions.explain: The spectral classes run O, B, A, F, G, K, M from the hottest (O) to the coolest (M) stars.

questions.q: What colour is a hot O-type star?
questions.explain: The hottest O-type stars appear blue, while the coolest M-type stars appear red.

questions.q: A Hertzsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram plots luminosity (or absolute magnitude) against which other property?
questions.explain: An H-R diagram plots luminosity or absolute magnitude against surface temperature (or spectral class).

questions.q: On the H-R diagram, where does the band of main sequence stars lie?
options: A diagonal band from top-left (hot, luminous) to bottom-right (cool, dim)
A horizontal band across the middle
questions.explain: Main sequence stars form a diagonal band running from hot, luminous stars at the top-left to cool, dim stars at the bottom-right.

questions.q: On the H-R diagram, temperature is plotted so that it does what across the horizontal axis?
options: Is shown on a logarithmic loop
questions.explain: By convention the temperature axis of an H-R diagram runs backwards, with the hottest stars on the left and temperature decreasing to the right.

questions.q: A white dwarf is hot but very dim. Whereabouts on the H-R diagram does it appear?
questions.explain: White dwarfs are hot (left) yet have low luminosity (bottom), so they sit in the lower-left region of the H-R diagram.

questions.q: Red giants appear in the top-right of the H-R diagram. What does this position tell you about them?
options: They are cool but very luminous
They are hot and very luminous
They are cool and very dim
They are hot but very dim
questions.explain: Top-right means low temperature (cool, right) combined with high luminosity, which is characteristic of red giants due to their large size.

questions.q: The Sun is a yellow main sequence star with a surface temperature of about 5,500-6,000 K. Which spectral class does it belong to?
questions.explain: The Sun is a G-type main sequence star, giving it its yellow colour and moderate surface temperature.

questions.q: Stars form from a large cloud of gas and dust in space. What is this cloud called?
questions.explain: Stars begin life when gravity pulls together the gas and dust of a nebula to form a protostar.

questions.q: What is the name given to the collapsing ball of gas and dust that forms before nuclear fusion begins in a new star?
questions.explain: A protostar is the early stage where gravity heats a collapsing cloud until fusion eventually starts.

questions.q: During its main sequence stage, a star releases energy by fusing which element?
questions.explain: Main sequence stars are stable because they fuse hydrogen nuclei into helium in their cores.

questions.q: A main sequence star stays stable in size because two forces are balanced. Which two?
options: Inward gravity and outward radiation/thermal pressure
Inward radiation pressure and outward gravity
Inward electric force and outward friction
questions.explain: Equilibrium is maintained when the inward pull of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure from the energy released by fusion.

questions.q: What is the correct end-of-life sequence for a low-mass star like the Sun after the main sequence?
options: Red giant, planetary nebula, white dwarf
questions.explain: A Sun-like star swells into a red giant, sheds a planetary nebula, and leaves behind a white dwarf.

questions.q: A star much more massive than the Sun ends its life in an enormous explosion. What is this explosion called?
questions.explain: High-mass stars become red supergiants and then explode as supernovae at the end of their lives.

questions.q: A star has about 15 times the mass of the Sun. Which two remnants could it leave behind after a supernova?
options: A neutron star or a black hole
A white dwarf or a planetary nebula
A red giant or a white dwarf
questions.explain: Depending on the remaining core mass, the supernova of a very massive star leaves a neutron star or a black hole.

questions.q: What does the luminosity of a star describe?
options: The total energy the star emits each second
How bright the star looks from Earth
questions.explain: Luminosity is the total power output of a star, independent of how far away it is.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek astronomer devised the original magnitude scale for the brightness of stars?
questions.explain: Hipparchus classified visible stars from magnitude 1 (brightest) to magnitude 6 (faintest).

questions.q: Absolute magnitude measures a star's brightness as it would appear from a standard distance of how many parsecs?
questions.explain: Absolute magnitude is defined as the apparent magnitude a star would have if it were placed exactly 10 parsecs away.

questions.q: On the magnitude scale, how does a star's number relate to how bright it appears?
options: The smaller (or more negative) the number, the brighter the star
The larger the number, the brighter the star
The number has no link to brightness
Only negative numbers indicate faint stars
questions.explain: The magnitude scale is inverted, so brighter objects have smaller or more negative magnitude values.

questions.q: What is the key difference between apparent magnitude and absolute magnitude?
options: Apparent magnitude is how bright a star looks from Earth, while absolute magnitude compares brightness at a fixed distance
Apparent magnitude is measured at 10 parsecs, while absolute magnitude is measured from Earth
They are two names for exactly the same quantity
Apparent magnitude describes colour and absolute magnitude describes size
questions.explain: Apparent magnitude depends on distance, whereas absolute magnitude standardises all stars to 10 parsecs for a fair comparison.

questions.q: A star has a measured parallax angle of 0.1 arcseconds. Using d = 1/p, what is its distance in parsecs?
questions.explain: Using d = 1/p = 1/0.1 = 10, the star lies 10 parsecs away.

questions.q: Two stars differ by exactly 5 magnitudes. By what factor do their apparent brightnesses differ?
questions.explain: A difference of 5 magnitudes corresponds to a brightness ratio of 100 on the magnitude scale.

questions.q: A nearby star shows a parallax angle of 0.5 arcseconds. What is its distance?
questions.explain: Using d = 1/p = 1/0.5 = 2 parsecs.
